vignette: Tom, a 47-year-old bus driver from North America, has experienced significant emotional distress since an encounter with the police five months ago. At the time of the incident, Tom had been driving his usual route through a busy downtown area when he noticed something unusual—a vehicle parked in front of his bus that seemed to be blocking traffic intentionally. As Tom approached the intersection, he could feel his heart racing as he realized there were two officers standing near the suspicious car. Suddenly, one officer motioned for him to pull over and park on the side of the road. Despite knowing he was a routine worker with nothing illicit about him, Tom felt a wave of panic as if he had done something wrong. The moment the police approached his bus, Tom's hands began to shake uncontrollably. He felt beads of sweat trickling down his forehead and could barely hear their questions over the roaring in his ears. The officers seemed abrupt and stern; they asked for identification and proceeded with a search of his vehicle. During this time, Tom found himself replaying worst-case scenarios in his head, imagining how he might lose his job or be wrongly accused. After what felt like an eternity but was only about 20 minutes, the officers concluded their investigation and allowed him to continue his route. However, Tom's world had shifted. Every day since that encounter, he has been hyperalert on the road, constantly scanning for signs of police presence or any suspicious activity. His mind frequently replays the incident, often at random moments throughout the day. At home, Tom struggles with insomnia because of these intrusive thoughts and nightmares involving similar confrontations with authority figures. He avoids driving through areas where he previously experienced this encounter, making his daily commute a source of great anxiety. When he sees police cars or hears sirens, he feels an immediate surge of fear and panic, his body tightening in anticipation of another stressful confrontation. His work as a bus driver has become increasingly challenging. Tom used to enjoy the routine and the sense of community he provided by transporting people safely around the city. Now, each trip fills him with dread. He finds himself overthinking simple interactions with passengers, fearing that something might trigger another police encounter or even cause suspicion among his colleagues. Socially, Tom has isolated himself more and more from friends and family. He struggles to open up about what happened because he fears being seen as paranoid or irrational. This avoidance of social situations exacerbates his feelings of isolation and further deepens his anxiety. Recently, Tom started experiencing intense physical reactions in seemingly benign situations where he perceives any form of authority presence. For example, a simple traffic stop for speeding left him trembling and unable to speak coherently with the officer until he managed to flee the scene in his car. These episodes have been particularly distressing as they interfere significantly with his ability to function both at work and in his personal life. Despite these challenges, Tom remains committed to his job because it provides a sense of stability and structure. He continues to push through each day, hoping that over time the memories will lessen their grip on him. However, the persistent anxiety and intrusive thoughts continue to dominate his daily experience, making it difficult for him to envision a future without these distressing symptoms. Tom’s story reflects the profound impact that one traumatic event can have on an individual's life, affecting nearly every aspect of his existence from work to social interactions to basic functioning.
